summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Costa Rica since 1971. The country adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first state in Central America to do so. Outright International and the ILGA World Database record the resulting legal framework covering conduct, gender recognition and legal protections.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Since May 2018, name changes on official identification are available through a simple, free procedure at the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones. From 2013 until then, transgender people could change their legal name only by judicial order. A 2016 bill that would have allowed change of both name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was not adopted.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation, while raising concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people. She recommended intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

No explicit visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travellers appears in current law. In December 2018, President Carlos Alvarado Quesada signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples.

In 2020 the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate-crime penalties. Penal Code article 112 provides up to 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation; article 380 provides 1 to 3 years for exclusion or segregation on that basis; article 386bis provides 3 to 10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail on that basis.

Official posture has been supportive. The government recognised the International Day Against Homophobia on 17 May from 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to support activities aimed at eradicating homophobia. President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial in May 2014. In 2018 President Alvarado issued a public apology for past state persecution, citing persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings. In June 2019 he became the first Costa Rican president to march in the San José pride parade, which drew about 100,000 participants.

There is countervailing pressure. A conversion-therapy bill has been stalled since its 2019 committee report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.

Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were formerly commonplace while same-sex conduct was technically legal. In 2000 the Supreme Court ruled that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis and violate constitutional rights.
tangentialFactors:
In 1990 the Minister of the Interior instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, warning that all such women would be stopped at the airport, in an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting. The policy is decades old and is not described as current.

When President Solís flew the rainbow flag in May 2014, lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties called it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending.

In 2000 the Supreme Court ruled that IVF is unconstitutional, a decision recorded in the context of partnership benefits.

The 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage. A 2012 poll found 60% of 18 to 34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples.
localsOnly:
The Justice Ministry announced in June 2017 that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility. Relocation to the facility matching gender identity is strictly voluntary and decided case by case with prison social workers and psychologists. A circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners; an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration; Spain's system was cited as the model, with protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016.

In June 2019 CRHoy reported that Stephanie, a trans woman serving about six years for drug-trafficking complicity, was held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility. She transitioned while incarcerated and said the prison offered only two options, man or woman. The Justice Ministry told CRHoy there were 23 transgender people in the national system at the time. Stephanie recounted identity-targeted abuse including a broomstick-handle rape at La Reforma in Alajuela witnessed by a custodian. Despite the 2017 choice policy, trans women were still held in men's facilities in 2019 and faced violence with custodial inaction.

In 2011 the Supreme Court reversed its 2008 ruling and allowed same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison.

In 1993 Universidad Internacional de las Américas was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff. When the Ministry of Education was informed, it said the policy would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33 and 70 if enforced.

Comprehensive sex education in Costa Rican public high schools is described as almost nonexistent because of opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the 2016 gender-recognition bill beyond its failure to be adopted is not sourced.

Enforcement of the 2020 hate-crime provisions is not documented in the available sources.

No source in the inventory documents border or airport screening practices specific to trans travellers.

The 1990 consular visa instruction is historical; no source indicates whether any comparable practice exists now.
